sources.limitations: Abstract only. The pessimistic conclusion is the authors' argument under their framework, not an independently established fact or universal rule for all finance research.
sources.metadata_notes: Published online October 2015; journal issue year 2016. Preserve the leading ellipsis in the article title.
sources.next_reading: Inspect the search universe, dependence assumptions, publication-selection assumptions and sensitivity of recommended cutoffs; compare directly with Jensen, Kelly and Pedersen.

sources.title: Does Academic Research Destroy Stock Return Predictability?
sources.version: Published journal article

urls.locator: Article information and Abstract; full-text URL redirected to abstract

sources.source_claim: The authors compare return predictability outside original study samples and after publication. They report declining performance and interpret their evidence as consistent with both data-mining effects and investors learning about mispricing from academic publications.
sources.project_relevance: Introduces out-of-sample economic performance and market adaptation as distinct explanations relevant to replication.
sources.limitations: Abstract only; numerical findings are intentionally omitted at the starter stage. Performance decay does not by itself establish that the original predictive relation was wholly spurious.
sources.metadata_notes: Published online October 2015; journal issue year 2016.
sources.next_reading: Audit predictor selection, portfolio construction, timing definitions, risk adjustment and identification of publication-informed trading.

sources.source_claim: The article proposes a double-bootstrap approach to calibrating false and missed discoveries while allowing different costs for the two kinds of error. Its opening discussion argues that attention to test power can change conclusions about manager selection.
sources.project_relevance: Provides a finance-specific bridge between multiple testing, power and the economic costs of decision errors.
sources.limitations: Opening sections only, not a full methodological review. Their definition of manager skill as positive alpha is explicitly distinguished from alternative equilibrium definitions.

sources.source_claim: The authors develop a hierarchical Bayesian model and international factor evidence that lead them to a substantially more favourable assessment of factor replication than earlier critiques. Their discussion attributes differences to sample construction, risk adjustment, the definition of replication and treatment of multiple testing.
sources.project_relevance: Supplies a recent substantive counterposition to pessimistic finance-replication claims and blanket threshold tightening.

sources.source_claim: Under their partial-identification framework and specified prior class, ex ante and ex post robust Bayes rules can differ, and randomisation can be optimal under both criteria. The conclusion acknowledges a restrictive prior and leaves the comparative merits of the criteria open.
sources.project_relevance: A counterweight to treating decision theory as a unique automatic replacement for testing: the choice of criterion and information assumptions remains consequential.
sources.limitations: Selected sections only; no proof verification or application replication. Results do not show that every decision requires randomisation or that one criterion is universally superior.
